newsitem.title: USA: U.S. continues Chile salmon dumping investigation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. continues Chile salmon dumping investigation.

text.p: The U.S. International Trade Commission ruled on Thursday that the Commerce Department should continue investigating allegations that Chile has been dumping salmon on the U.S. market.
The three-member panel found that accusations filed by U.S. fresh salmon producers merit further investigation and that fast growing Chilean imports may have hurt the U.S. salmon industry.

"There is a reasonable indication that a U.S. industry is materially injured by reason of imports of fresh Atlantic salmon from Chile that are allegedly subsidised and sold at less than fair value," the ITC said in a statement.
The Commerce Department will investigate the allegations made by salmon producers in Maine and Washington to determine whether dumping occurred and if so, how much, the ITC said.
Commerce is expected to announce its initial findings on or about September 5, according to the ITC.

If Commerce finds evidence to support the claims, the ITC would determine whether the dumping harmed the U.S. salmon industry. Commerce would then decide whether to impose tariffs and other surcharges on the Chilean imports.
Chilean officials have denied that their salmon is government subsidised and therefore unfair competition.
They say Chile produces a better and cheaper product that has rapidly gained consumers in the United States, capturing 40 percent of the U.S. market.
Chilean exports of salmon and trout to the United States have soared from just $3.4 million in 1986 to $177 million in 1996.
Chile is now the top foreign supplier of salmon to the United States, but Chilean producers fear punitive tariffs would force them out of the market.
Chile is the world's second largest salmon producer after Norway, which lost its share of the U.S. market due to tariffs imposed after the ITC ruled against Norwegian salmon in 1991.
